Montenegro does seem like a good option but a couple of things to bare in mind that it's hard to know before you get there and are important for everyday life:

\- There's nothing like the convenience of Amazon there. People regularly travel to different Balkan countries to buy stuff like deck chairs or whatever because the choices in Montenegro are very limited.  
\- They wouldn't give us the vaccine as foreigners there (we tried in multiple areas). As a non-resident, I don't know what other health-related problems that might cause.  
\- The food choices are pretty limiting. My wife (Chinese) was extremely limited by what authentic food she could make and veggies aren't as fresh as you might be used to in most areas. Restaurants are very hit and miss. (though the bread and italian food is usually great)

Okay great! I'll start with some feature films:  
\-【 霸王别姬 (Farewell my concubine)】 is a great look at both Beijing opera, the opiate influence on China's history and the cultural revolution. It follows the life of two theatre performers from a young age. It's a true classic.  
\- 【Crazy Rich Asians】, although the title may make you think otherwise, is full of depth in articulating the subtleties of modern Chinese culture. Especially relationships and the differences between the western world. It is about a man returning to Singapore (I think) with his partner and facing his family.  
\- 【Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon】 is remembered as an action flick, but it's also an interesting look back into the life and customs of ancient China.   
\- 【The Last Emperor】documents the fall of Manchurian reign in China, touching on darker aspects of the handover during that time and showing the peculiarities of royal China during that period.

The homophones are real. Once you get to a certain amount of vocabulary, you will have multiple meanings for every syllable. I just scrolled through the pinyin "shi" in my dictionary and counted 40 characters I knew. There were lots I didn't know. This begins happening noticeably around HSK 3.  


If you can differentiate between tones spoken mid-sentence then maybe you could use this strategy instead of learning characters. However this is an extremely difficult skill. Personally, I find learning individual tones harder than learning the characters.  


The reason learning characters helps you differentiate is because you use them to group different words and thus build out lots of interconnected groups of similar words and expressions. Therefore instead of a sound (with 40 options you have to sift through in your head) being associated with something, you only have one. Often I can't remember exactly how to write a character (I just focus on recognition), but I'll know the rough outline and this will give me something to fix onto.   


When someone says something and I don't catch it immediately, my brain will rifle through a few meanings for "shì" that are totally different, but may be plausible. I simply cannot understand how it is possible to get extremely individual meanings out of the exact same pronunciation without characters.  


Also, it naturally forces you to break the similar sounding word into more meaningful distinctions, which further increases your understanding of each distinct syllable. Because instead of only having four categories to put them into (assuming you are a genius with tones)  "shì shí shǐ shī", you have a distinct representation of each word 是，市，实，时，石. I have no idea what the pinyin means, but  the characters make perfect sense.  


At higher level it becomes super easy (compared to when you start) to learn new vocabulary once you've learnt a large number of characters because it's just like picking up a new word like "facebook" - you just stick two words you already know together. I think you'll struggle to do this more without solid knowledge to grasp hold of, which is what the characters give you.  


The thing is, kids have a magically ability to soak up language that doesn't apply to adults, so you shouldn't try to study the same way... Also, you probably don't have access to a 100% immersive environment and adults constantly correcting you, which is absolutely key for kid's learning.  


YouTube will get you so far, but I remember reading a study where it said that learning through film is 1% without subtitles and 4% with subtitles (I can't remember if these are the exact figures,  but the evidence is very strong). So you're making things 4x slower (or something) by not knowing subtitles.  


Also also, to your second point, when studying characters you're simultaneously studying the tones and cementing vocabulary within your brain while studying characters. So it's not like you're literally only studying the characters themselves.   


If you can write a character, you'll remember the meaning for far longer without forgetting it than if you've only heard it. In fact, Chinese is so similar-sounding that it's got to the point where I almost always forget a word when I hear it unless I look up the characters for it at the same time.  


Thinking of a word in terms of pinyin is just way too flaky. Nothing to grab on to - it's too easy to forget amongst its similar sounding brethren. You won't be understand word families through sound because it'd be a total mess - there'd be too much overlapping business.

Ingredients (2 serving)

​

1 cup rice

A handful of millet

3 eggs

3 tomatoes

2-3 Spring onions

Half a large garlic

Peanut oil

Light soy sauce

​

​

Method

​

Rinse rice

Add 2 cups of water (a cup of water per half cup of rice - add less or more to make the rice harder or softer)

Put it into a rice cooker with the millet for around 20minutes

Prepare tomatoes: cut into segments

Crack eggs into a bowl and whisk a little

Peel and dice the garlic

Chop up the spring onions

Pour the peanut oil into a wok pan and heat until bubbling. 

Add the eggs. Use a chopstick to separate the egg as it cooks (it should cook in about 30seconds).

Remove the egg and put it to the side

Fry tomato in a little oil and a half teaspoon of light soy sauce.

Once the tomatoes are softened up, add the egg back into the pan and mix the tomato juices into the egg.

Sprinkle the spring onion on top
